--- title: "Exploring the data first" description: "A check order for a new dataset, and the plots and counts that find sentinel values, impossible depths, messy categories and missing values with a pattern." order: 4 categories: [eda, data-preparation] --- ## A model will not tell you the data is wrong A model fits whatever it is given. It will not say that a salinity column holds `-999`: it reports a plausible score and builds on a mean salinity no ocean has. This page gives an order for checking a new dataset, and runs it on the raw survey file, whose problems take minutes to see by looking and are invisible in a model's output afterwards. The aim of this first look is not to find results but to find what is wrong. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Check in a fixed order A fixed order makes it harder to skip a check. This one runs roughly cheapest first: ::: {.diagram} ![A check order for a new dataset. Each step looks for a different kind of problem; the last, comparing groups such as vessels or observers, is the one that finds a faulty instrument.](img/check-order.svg){fig-alt="Seven numbered cards joined by arrows. 1 Shape and types: rows and columns, and how each was read. 2 Missing values: how many, and do they follow a pattern. 3 One column: its range, spikes and impossible values. 4 Every category: every level, with its count. 5 Two columns: relationships you did not expect. 6 The outcome: its spread, and how rare each class is. 7 By group: vessel, observer, year, gear. A note says step 7 is the one most often skipped, and the one that catches a faulty instrument."} ::: The rest of the page runs the steps that find something in the raw survey file (see [The coastal survey](the-coastal-survey.qmd)). ## The ranges show impossible values The quickest useful check of all: the smallest, average and largest value of every numeric column, read as a scientist would. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw <- load_coastal_survey_raw() raw |> summarise(across(where(is.numeric), list(min = \(x) min(x, na.rm = TRUE), mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), max = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))) |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", "stat"), names_sep = "_(?=[^_]+$)") |> pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = value) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|variable | min| mean| max| |:-----------------|-------:|-------:|-------:| |survey_year | 2018.00| 2020.49| 2023.00| |longitude | 140.01| 141.26| 142.50| |latitude | 41.00| 42.00| 43.00| |depth_m | 5.00| 102.68| 1581.00| |temperature_c | -999.00| -1.29| 16.03| |salinity_psu | -999.00| 2.24| 34.96| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 0.07| 1.42| 13.75| |abundance | 0.00| 3.88| 40.00| |catch_weight_kg | 0.00| 1.37| 13.26|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_raw raw = load_coastal_survey_raw() (raw.select_dtypes("number") .agg(["min", "mean", "max"]) # pandas skips missing values by default .T .round(2) .reset_index(names="variable")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | variable | min | mean | max | |:------------------|--------:|--------:|--------:| | survey_year | 2018 | 2020.49 | 2023 | | longitude | 140.01 | 141.26 | 142.5 | | latitude | 41 | 42 | 43 | | depth_m | 5 | 102.68 | 1581 | | temperature_c | -999 | -1.29 | 16.03 | | salinity_psu | -999 | 2.24 | 34.96 | | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 0.07 | 1.42 | 13.75 | | abundance | 0 | 3.88 | 40 | | catch_weight_kg | 0 | 1.37 | 13.26 | ::: ::: ::: Three things should stop you: - **Salinity has a minimum of −999 and a mean of 2.24.** No ocean is that fresh. Some instrument or export wrote `-999` to mean "missing", a **sentinel value**, and because it is a number nothing complained. Temperature has it too. - **Depth reaches 1581 m** on a shelf survey whose stations are all shallower than 200 m. - **Chlorophyll** has 52 values recorded as `NA`, the honest way to record a missing value. A histogram makes the sentinel impossible to miss, and a count by season shows the missing chlorophyll has a pattern: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_sentinel <- ggplot(raw, aes(salinity_psu)) + geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + annotate("text", x = -999, y = 30, label = paste0("−999\n(", sum(raw$salinity_psu == -999), " rows)"), hjust = -0.15, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.5) + labs(x = "Salinity (PSU)", y = "Stations", title = "A number that is not a measurement") p_missing <- raw |> group_by(season) |> summarise(missing = 100 * mean(is.na(chlorophyll_mg_m3))) |> mutate(season = fct_reorder(season, missing)) |> ggplot(aes(missing, season)) + geom_col(fill = ml_palette[["orange"]], width = 0.62) + geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(missing), "%")), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.6) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) + labs(x = "Chlorophyll missing (%)", y = NULL, title = "Missing, but not at random") p_sentinel + p_missing ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: every salinity value. The real ocean is the narrow cluster near 34; the bar at −999 is missing values disguised as a number. Right: chlorophyll is missing far more often in winter, a pattern that can bias results.](exploratory-analysis_files/figure-html/fig-damage-1.png){#fig-damage fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel is a histogram of salinity with a bar at minus 999 and a narrow cluster of real values near 34, separated by a wide empty gap. The right panel is a bar chart of the percentage of missing chlorophyll by season: about 1 percent in autumn, 2 in spring, 4 in summer and 19 in winter.' width=1700} ::: ::: ## Categories hide spelling variants Count every level of every category, not a sample of them: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw |> count(substrate, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|substrate | n| |:---------|---:| |mud | 163| |Sand | 100| |gravel | 95| |SAND | 82| |Mud | 79| |muddy | 72| |sandy | 66| |sand | 57| |Gravel | 46| |Rock | 21| |rocky | 20| |rock | 14|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} raw["substrate"].value_counts().reset_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | substrate | count | |:------------|--------:| | Sand | 100 | | mud | 88 | | SAND | 82 | | Mud | 79 | | mud | 75 | | muddy | 72 | | sandy | 66 | | sand | 57 | | gravel | 49 | | Gravel | 46 | | gravel | 46 | | Rock | 21 | | rocky | 20 | | rock | 14 | ::: ::: ::: Four kinds of seabed, 12 spellings. A model treats `Sand`, `SAND`, `sand` and `sandy` as four unrelated categories, and splits the evidence for sand four ways. ## The outcome can be rare ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw |> count(rare_species) |> mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|rare_species | n| percent| |:------------|---:|-------:| |no | 772| 94.7| |yes | 43| 5.3|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} counts = raw["rare_species"].value_counts().reset_index() counts["percent"] = (100 * counts["count"] / counts["count"].sum()).round(1) counts ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | rare_species | count | percent | |:---------------|--------:|----------:| | no | 772 | 94.7 | | yes | 43 | 5.3 | ::: ::: ::: A rare species is present at only 5% of stations. A model that always answers "absent" would be right 95% of the time, so any model for it has to beat that. [Splitting the data](splitting-data.qmd) returns to rare classes. ## Groups reveal a faulty instrument Comparing the two vessels, with the sentinel values left out: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw |> filter(salinity_psu != -999) |> group_by(vessel) |> summarise(stations = n(), mean_salinity = round(mean(salinity_psu), 2), mean_temperature = round(mean(temperature_c[temperature_c != -999]), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|vessel | stations| mean_salinity| mean_temperature| |:----------|--------:|-------------:|----------------:| |RV Kaiyo | 437| 33.75| 8.72| |RV Tsubasa | 353| 34.13| 8.41|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} valid = raw.assign( temperature_c=raw["temperature_c"].where(raw["temperature_c"] != -999) ).query("salinity_psu != -999") (valid.groupby("vessel") .agg(stations=("salinity_psu", "size"), mean_salinity=("salinity_psu", "mean"), mean_temperature=("temperature_c", "mean")) .round(2) .reset_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | vessel | stations | mean_salinity | mean_temperature | |:-----------|-----------:|----------------:|-------------------:| | RV Kaiyo | 437 | 33.75 | 8.72 | | RV Tsubasa | 353 | 34.13 | 8.41 | ::: ::: ::: The two vessels differ by 0.38 PSU in mean salinity, with no matching difference in temperature. Two ships sampling the same shelf should not disagree like that: one instrument is off, and every plot that pooled the two vessels hid it. ## Each finding is a decision The checks found six problems. None is fixed automatically; each needs a decision from someone who knows how the data was collected: | Finding | The decision it forces | | --- | --- | | `-999` in salinity (25 rows) and temperature (8) | Convert to missing, then decide how to handle missing values | | Depths up to 1581 m | Error or real? Correct, drop or flag | | 12 spellings of four substrates | Standardise, without merging a real distinction | | Chlorophyll missing in 19% of winter stations | Dropping those rows would delete a large part of winter | | Rare species at 5% | Always answering "absent" already scores 95% | | One vessel reads 0.38 PSU high | Correct it, model it, or leave salinity out | [Missing values and outliers](missing-values-and-outliers.qmd) makes these decisions. Some errors will survive any amount of looking: a depth recorded ten times too deep is obvious at 1,500 m but not at 150 m. Cleaning reduces errors; it does not remove them all. This first look uses every row, including those that will later test a model. That is unavoidable, since data cannot be cleaned unseen, and harmless as long as it stays about data quality. Choices about the outcome and the model belong to the training data alone; [Avoiding information leakage](information-leakage.qmd) draws the line. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A first look is a search for problems. Its output is a list of decisions. - Read the range of every numeric column: sentinel values such as −999 and impossible depths show at once. - Count every level of every category: spelling variants split one category into several. - Ask whether missing values follow a pattern, such as a season; patterned gaps can bias results. - Compare groups such as vessels or observers: that is where a faulty instrument hides. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Run `skimr::skim(raw)` and `naniar::vis_miss(raw)`. What do they show faster than the code above, and what do they miss? 2. Take the depths above 250 m and divide them by ten. Do the corrected values fit the relationship between depth and temperature in the rest of the survey? That kind of evidence turns a guess about an error into a defensible correction.
